name: ITALY
lead: Italy is shaped exactly like a tall boot kicking a football — that football is Sicily. Wedged between the Alps and the Mediterranean, it gave the world pizza, pasta, the Roman Empire, and the Renaissance. Sixty million Italians live where ancient ruins sit beside buzzing cafés, and lunch is always taken seriously.
geo: Italy is a long peninsula stretching into the Mediterranean, with the Alps forming a snowy wall to the north. Two large islands — Sicily and Sardinia — belong to Italy, and two tiny nations (Vatican City and San Marino) sit entirely inside its borders.

The Apennine Mountains run like a spine down the peninsula, and Italy has two active volcanoes: fiery Etna on Sicily and restless Vesuvius near Naples. The flat, fertile Po Valley in the north is the country's breadbasket.
animals: The grey wolf, once nearly gone, has bounced back to over 3,000 animals roaming the Apennines. The Marsican brown bear — a rare subspecies — numbers just around 60 individuals sheltering in Abruzzo National Park.
Italy's seas hold bluefin tuna, swordfish, and loggerhead turtles nesting on southern beaches. The tiny Giara wild horse of Sardinia stands barely a metre tall and is found nowhere else on Earth.
culture: Italians treat food as art: each region has its own recipes, and using the wrong pasta shape is a genuine offence. Espresso is drunk standing at a bar in under a minute; Sunday dinner stretches for hours.

Opera was born in Italy around 1600, and football (calcio) is practically a religion. Italian fashion houses, sports cars, and ceramic tiles are copied worldwide. The afternoon riposo is still sacred in smaller towns.
history: Rome grew from a village (753 BC legend) into an empire ruling from Scotland to Mesopotamia. When it collapsed in AD 476, Italy split into rival city-states — Florence, Venice, Milan — each funding artists like Leonardo and Michelangelo.

The Renaissance (1400–1600) made Italy the art capital of the world. The country only unified in 1861, making modern Italy younger than the United States. After World War II it rebuilt into one of the world's largest economies.
wows: Italy holds more UNESCO World Heritage Sites than any country — 59 as of 2024.
Vatican City, surrounded by Rome, is the world's smallest country at 0.44 km².
Roman harbour concrete built 2,000 years ago still stands intact underwater today.
Italy produces more wine than any country — over 4.9 billion litres every year.
The Colosseum held up to 80,000 spectators and had a retractable awning for shade.
Italian is the closest living language to Latin — about 60% mutually intelligible.
Mount Etna has been erupting on and off for at least 500,000 years.

myths.fact: Pasta existed in Italy before Marco Polo — Arab traders likely introduced dried pasta to Sicily around the 9th century, decades before his 1295 return.
Caesar was never emperor — he was a dictator of the Republic, assassinated in 44 BC. His adopted son Augustus became the first true emperor.
